1:
The psalm opens the whole Psalter with a benediction, and the witnesses hear in that first word the note that governs everything after: the blessedness of the man who has withdrawn from the company of the wicked. The reformed John Gill renders it as an exclamation, "O the blessednesses of the man," a plural that makes him doubly blessed, a thrice happy man, blessed in things temporal and spiritual, in this world and the world to come; and he notes that the psalm begins as Christ's Sermon on the Mount begins, with the praises of the truly happy. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the same Hebrew: ashrey is plural, "O the blessedness of the man!", and haish is emphatic, "that man," the one among a thousand who lives for the very end for which God made him.

Both the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and Clarke trace a double gradation in the verse: three characters of evil that mount in wickedness, and three postures that settle ever deeper into it. The ungodly, Henry says, are the unsettled, who cast off the fear of God and walk by no certain rule; the sinners break out into open rebellion and set up sin as their trade; the scornful, worst of all, set their mouths against the heavens and make a jest of sin, for none reach the height of vice at once. Clarke sharpens the philology: reshaim, the unjust who withhold from God and man their due; chattaim, who miss the mark and overpass the prohibited bound; letsim, the mockers and deriders, at least deists who turn revelation into ridicule. And the postures, walk, stand, sit, mark the descent, for the ungodly has his counsel, the sinner his way, the scorner his seat. The reformed John Calvin and John Wesley read the same steps, Calvin taking counsel for the wickedness not yet openly shown, the way for the customary manner of life, and the seat for the obduracy bred by habit; Wesley agreeing that standing is more than walking and sitting more than standing, and the scornful the worst of sinners.

Against this the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott enters a caution: the apparent gradation, he holds, was a necessity of the rhythm rather than a studied epitome of the whole history of sin, though he grants the three terms their distinct senses, the ungodly restless and wanting self-control (Isa. 57:20), the sinners general wrong-doers, the scornful a proverbial class whom Aquila calls mockers, Symmachus impostors, and the Septuagint and Vulgate a pestilence; and he suggests that seat may rather be assembly. Calvin, too, doubts whether the three Hebrew nouns really mount, except perhaps in the last. Furthest from all these stands the latin-fathers Augustine, who reads the whole verse of Christ, the Lord Man, who unlike the man of earth hath not gone away in the counsel of the ungodly, came in the way of sinners by being born as sinners are yet stood not therein, and never sat in the seat of pestilence, which he takes for the pride of earthly rule, or for a hurtful doctrine whose word spreads as a canker.
2:
The verse turns from what the blessed man shuns to what he loves, and the witnesses gather around the delight and the meditation that mark him out. The reformed John Gill is careful about which law is meant: not the law of nature, now greatly impaired by sin, nor the law of Moses considered as a fiery law that works wrath and condemns, unless it be taken as it lies in the hands of Christ, who is the end of it; but rather the Scriptures as far as they were then written, and particularly the five books of Moses, called the Law and the Testimony, inspired by God and delightful to read and to hear explained. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads "his delight" from the Hebrew chephtso, his will, desire, and affection, every motive of the heart set on the side of God's truth; he takes up the law as the rule of his life, and is no forgetful hearer but a doer of the word, feeding on it as the sincere milk by which he grows. And because his heart is in it, the work is not occasional but perpetual, by day and by night.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the wording on both sides. The opening "but" is an elliptical Hebrew expression implying a strong contrast, "nay but," "on the contrary," swinging the reader from the negative portrait to the positive; and the clause is better rendered "to the law of Jehovah is his inclination," the Hebrew verb meaning primarily to bend. The word translated "meditate," he shows, means literally to murmur, used of the cooing of a dove (Isa. 38:14), of men lamenting (Isa. 16:7), of a lion growling over its prey (Isa. 31:4), and of muttered charms (Isa. 8:19), so that the blessed man's meditation is a low and constant rehearsing of the word under his breath, a picture Ellicott ties to the charge given to Joshua (Josh. 1:8).

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry defines that meditation itself: to meditate in God's word is to discourse with ourselves concerning the great things contained in it, with a close application of mind and a fixedness of thought, till we are suitably affected and feel the savour and power of them in our hearts; and this by day and night, the thoughts interwoven with the business of every day and the repose of every night. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley gathers the whole force of that phrase into a line: not seldom and slightly, but diligently and constantly. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the negative holiness of the first verse is grounded in this positive affection, and that a man's separation from the counsel of the ungodly is kept only by a heart perpetually occupied, waking and sleeping, with the law it has learned to love.
3:
At the heart of the psalm stands its great image of the flourishing tree, and the witnesses linger over every branch of it. The reformed John Gill reads the opening vau as "for then shall he be," the simile proving the man's blessedness: he is like a tree, not a dry or fruitless one but a green and flourishing tree, an olive, a palm, a cedar of Lebanon, and above all a tree "planted," not one that grows of itself in the wild, but one removed from its native soil and set elsewhere; so the believer is broken off the wild olive and grafted into the good, planted in Christ and in the church, of which the transplanting of Israel into Canaan was an emblem. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the same word: not a tree growing wild, however luxuriant, but one carefully cultivated, its soil and situation chosen; and he unfolds "the rivers of water," palgey mayim, as the streams or channels of eastern irrigation, turned off and on at pleasure by a man's foot, the watering of the land with the foot of Deut. 11:10. Its fruit comes in its season, expectation never disappointed; its leaf does not wither, the unsullied profession that ever shows faith by works; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper, as a healthy tree is always striking deeper root.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would render "And he" more exactly as "So is he," and sets the figure in its eastern climate, where all vegetation depends on nearness to a stream (Ps. 92:12; Jer. 17:7-8); he even asks what kind of tree the poet had in mind, dismissing Dean Stanley's oleander for its want of fruit and settling on the palm as best meeting every condition, and he renders the obscure last clause "all that he doeth he maketh to prosper." The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon dwells on the security of the planting, a tree chosen and cared for and kept from the final uprooting of Matt. 15:13, and on the never-failing supply, "by the rivers of water," so that if one river should fail he has another, the rivers of pardon and grace and promise and communion. Yet Spurgeon adds a caution against reading the prospering by sight, for the tried believer may, like Jacob, feel for a time that all these things are against him. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley sums the leaf that does not wither: the good man's happiness is not short and transitory but ever green and flourishing. The witnesses do not divide; together they read the tree as the very portrait of a life rooted in the word, fruitful, evergreen, and prospering under the hand that planted it.
4:
"The ungodly are not so" — the witnesses seize on the abrupt antithesis, and on the chaff to which the wicked are likened. The reformed John Gill draws the contrast point for point: the ungodly walk in the counsel of ungodly men, stand in the way of sinners, and sit in the seat of the scornful, having no delight in the law; and if they are like trees at all, they are like dry trees without sap or verdure, wild olives on a heath in a parched land, fit only for the fire. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the Septuagint emphatically repeat the phrase, "Not so the ungodly; they are not so," and unfolds the figure of the chaff: the very lightest of the chaff, the dust the owner of the floor desires driven away, of no worth in God's account however highly they value themselves, light and vain, with no solidity, blown to and fro by every wind of temptation; and their end is written in it, for the wrath of God will drive them away as the wind the chaff, and he is coming whose fan is in his hand to purge his floor (Matt. 3:12).

The wesleyan-arminian voices supply the husbandry behind the image. Adam Clarke notes that the Vulgate and Septuagint double the negation and add a clause, "Not so the ungodly, not so; they shall be like the dust which the wind scatters," and describes the eastern winnowing: the grain thrown up against the wind falls nearly perpendicular while the light chaff is carried off, so the ungodly and their works are borne away to destruction by the wind of God's judgments. John Wesley reads the chaff as the restless and unquiet, whose seeming felicity has no firm foundation but quickly vanishes and flees away. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the rendering "Not so the ungodly" and the picture of a people winnowed out of the society of the true Israel by the fan of God's judgment, an image so frequent in the prophets as almost to have become a poetical commonplace (Hab. 3:12; Joel 3:14). And the puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon marks who these "ungodly" are, the beginners in evil, the least offensive of sinners, the quiet moralists who neglect their God; if even their estate is thus hopeless, how much worse the doom of open sinners and shameless infidels. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the chaff has neither root, weight, nor stability, and that the very wind which is nothing to the rooted tree sweeps the rootless away.
5:
The verse pronounces the doom of the ungodly in the court of God, that they shall not stand in the judgment nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous, and here the witnesses part over the very sense of "stand." The reformed John Gill takes it of both a temporal and the final judgment, following the Targum and Kimchi for the last great day: the wicked will indeed be arraigned before the judgment seat, but they shall not stand with the righteous at Christ's right hand, nor stand with any holy confidence; they will not be acquitted but will fall, condemned to everlasting punishment. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch ground the "therefore" in the chaff just described: precisely because of their inner worthlessness and instability the ungodly cannot stand in the judgment, the mishpat of just recompense to which God brings every man with all his words and works. And the other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, marks the deliberate contrast with the first verse, that those who chose the assembly of the scornful will have no place in the assembly of the good, reading "shall not stand" as properly "shall not rise," like our phrase "shall not hold up his head," the self-convicted sinner shrinking away like the man without a wedding garment (Matt. 22:12).

Here a genuine difference opens. The Septuagint and Vulgate render the clause "shall not rise again," as though with thought of an after-state, and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports that some among Jews and Christians built on that reading the opinion that the impious will never be raised at all but simply annihilated, a notion he dismisses as unworthy of refutation, holding the plain sense to be that when the wicked come to be judged they shall be condemned, having nothing to plead. So the witnesses part over whether the verse denies the ungodly a standing, an acquittal, a lifted head, in a judgment they must all alike face, as Gill, Ellicott, and Wesley hold, or whether the versional "shall not rise" touches the resurrection itself, as the Greek and Latin suggested and Clarke was concerned to correct. John Wesley keeps it simplest, that not to stand is not to endure the trial, in the great and general judgment of the world. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon closes on the second line: no evil man shall dwell in heaven, for every congregation on earth is mixed, tares among the wheat and one devil in every church, but into the congregation of the righteous above no unrenewed soul shall enter, a sinner being as out of his element there as a fish upon a tree. The witnesses converge at last on the terror of the exclusion, however they construe the standing.
6:
The psalm ends by laying the two ways side by side and tracing them to their root in God himself, that the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous but the way of the ungodly shall perish, and the witnesses agree that everything turns on the word "knoweth." The reformed John Gill insists it means far more than bare omniscience, for in that sense God knows the way of the wicked too; here to know is to approve, to love, and to take delight in the righteous man's way of faith and holiness, his walk in Christ, his sacrifices of prayer and praise that meet with acceptance. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads "knoweth" as approveth, the "aloweth" of Coverdale, and derives the very name of the righteous, tsaddikim, from a root meaning to give even weight, the men who render to all their due, the opposite of the reshaim of the first verse who withhold right from all; and such are under the continual eye of God's providence, who knows the way they take and defends them in body and soul. John Wesley sums it the same way: God approves, loves, and delights in them, and will therefore recompense them, while the way of the wicked, all their designs and courses, shall come to nothing.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott glosses "knoweth" as recognises with discriminative discernment and appreciation (Ps. 31:7; John 10:14), and finds the perishing "way" explained by the parallel that the desire of the wicked shall perish (Ps. 112:10), an image he likens to Job's picture of a treacherous stream that dries up and vanishes in the heat (Job 6:18). The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon renders the Hebrew as a continuous action, "the LORD is knowing the way of the righteous," constantly watching it even when it runs through mist and darkness, so that the tried man may say, "when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold" (Job 23:10); but the way of the ungodly perishes with him, for the righteous carves his name upon the rock while the wicked does but plough the sea, and the place that knew him shall know him no more. The witnesses do not divide. They gather at the close upon a single confession, that the whole difference between the blessed man and the chaff lies in this, that the LORD owns and keeps the one way and lets the other come to nothing, so that the psalm which opened with a blessing shuts with the quiet certainty of a God who marks and guards the path of his own.
